title: MAC both ways on a host link, and know when you don't know

blocks.text: The acquirer's host MACs every message in both directions, and its spec, copied into the class comment of `src/main/java/com/example/practice/MacLink.java`, differs from the one on the page in one point: when a message has any field above 64, the MAC goes in field 128 instead of 64. Your reversals carry field 90, so they are such messages.
Two problems reached operations this month:

items: every reversal the client sends is answered `63`, security violation;
on a day the host's MAC key was being changed, a few hundred cardholders were told "declined" for purchases that their banks show as paid.

blocks.text: Finish the four methods marked `TODO`: `macField`, `macInput`, `sign` and `outcomeOf`. `send` already signs a copy of the request and passes the response, or `null` when none came, to `outcomeOf`. About twenty lines in total.

The tests use a real `JCESecurityModule` with a test MAC key on each side and the course's `iso87ascii.xml` packager on every message. The host behind the fake `MUX` checks your MAC with its own code, answers `63` when it doesn't verify, and declines amounts over 500.00. Some tests change its answer on the way back.

cases.says: a purchase goes out with a MAC the host verifies, and the host's signed approval is an approval
a signed decline whose MAC verifies is a decline, and the caller's request is left unsigned
a message with fields above 64, such as a reversal with field 90, carries its MAC in field 128, and the response is checked the same way
a response whose MAC does not verify proves nothing, so the outcome is unknown rather than a decline
a response with no MAC is handled like one with a wrong MAC, not accepted
no answer leaves the outcome unknown, the same as a response that cannot be trusted

origin.section: 7.6 A Response That Fails Its MAC Is an Unknown Outcome, Not a Decline

concepts: A response with a wrong or missing MAC proves nothing, so the outcome is unknown, as with no answer: reverse and alert, never report a decline.
The MAC covers the packed message as sent, with the MAC field's bit set and its own bytes left out, computed on a copy so a received MAC is never overwritten.
